cards.front: What does it mean that inheritance is transitive?
cards.back: If Sedan extends Car and Car extends Vehicle, Sedan is also a Vehicle
cards.extra: The chain is real: Sedan inherits from Vehicle indirectly, and a Sedan reference can be assigned to a Vehicle variable.

cards.back: Yes, implicitly — Object is the root of every hierarchy
cards.extra: class Cat {} is really class Cat extends Object. That is why toString, equals and hashCode are available on everything.

cards.front: Are private superclass members inherited by a subclass?
cards.back: They exist in the subclass instance but are not accessible from the subclass's code
cards.extra: So the state is carried along, but only reachable through inherited public or protected accessors.

cards.front: Is a package-private (default) superclass member inherited?
cards.back: Only if the subclass is in the same package
cards.extra: A subclass in another package loses access entirely — protected is the modifier that grants package-plus-subclass access.

cards.front: Can a Java class extend more than one class?
cards.back: No — a single superclass only; multiple inheritance of type comes from interfaces
cards.extra: The diamond problem of C++ is avoided by restricting classes to one parent; interfaces carry no state.

cards.front: What is upcasting, and does it need a cast?
cards.back: Assigning a subclass instance to a superclass variable — implicit, no cast needed
cards.extra: Animal a = new Cat(); always works, because the instance really is an Animal.

cards.front: What is downcasting, and when does it fail?
cards.back: Assigning a superclass reference to a subclass variable with an explicit cast — it compiles, but throws ClassCastException if the object is not actually that type
cards.extra: The compiler cannot know the runtime type, so the check moves to run time. instanceof first, or use a pattern-matching cast.

cards.front: Why annotate an overriding method with @Override?
cards.back: So the compiler verifies that a method really is overriding something
cards.extra: A typo in the signature that would otherwise silently create a new method becomes a compile error instead.

cards.front: When should a base class be abstract rather than concrete?
cards.back: When it is only a home for reusable code and nobody should instantiate it
cards.extra: Making it abstract prevents new Base() outright, which is stronger than a comment saying not to.
